title: Jameson Taillon’s early exit is the latest issue for Cubs’ rotation
content:
CHICAGO — Already dealing with a fragile pitching situation, the Chicago Cubs will place Jameson Taillon on the injured list after he exited “Sunday Night Baseball” in the second inning with a strained left hamstring, one of many issues for a team in free fall.

The state of the Cubs is such that Taillon’s replacement, Javier Assad, pitched 6 ⅓ scoreless innings at Wrigley Field on short notice, receiving a standing ovation from the crowd of 36,317, and the San Francisco Giants still walked away with a 2-1 victory after 10 innings.

Taillon is scheduled to undergo an MRI on Monday to determine the severity of the injury and an estimated recovery period.

Taillon motioned toward the home dugout after walking Matt Chapman, the only batter he would face in the second inning. After a brief mound visit with Cubs manager Craig Counsell and an athletic trainer, Taillon walked off the field and Assad jogged in from the bullpen.

Foreshadowing this kind of possibility, the Cubs had limited Assad to one inning in his last appearance at Triple-A Iowa, and promoted him to Chicago before Saturday’s game. But both Counsell and Taillon indicated that this hamstring issue popped up suddenly.

The Cubs are now 0-8-1 in their last nine series, a downward spiral that has turned their two 10-game winning streaks earlier this season into distant memories.

“It’s not what any of us expected,” Taillon said. “It’s just a matter of what it’s going to take to get us back to being that good team. I don’t doubt that we can be that good team. But that being said, it would be nice to see it here soon.

“Unforunately, now I’m hurt, but before that, I wasn’t helping the cause. And there’s been some struggles all around the room. I don’t think any of us doubt what we’re capable of. But, yeah, we’ve just put ourselves in a bad spot.”

Taillon, 34, is in the final season of the four-year, $68 million contract he signed as a free agent, part of the group acquired to bring playoff baseball back to Wrigleyville. He set the tone in the wild-card clincher against the San Diego Padres last October, and he successfully handled another elimination game in the next round as the Cubs extended that playoff series against the Milwaukee Brewers.

That momentum, however, hasn’t carried over into this season. By allowing one run in his one inning against the Giants, Taillon’s ERA crept up to 5.19. He’s allowed 20 home runs in 13 starts, a sign of his recent lack of execution and shrinking margin for error.

Still, Taillon is viewed as a dependable starter, a student of the game and a widely respected player within the clubhouse.

The Cubs (34-32) went into this year viewing the depth of their rotation as a strength, but it has substantially eroded since April, when potential ace Cade Horton underwent season-ending surgery on his right elbow.

Late May or early June was once the targeted date range for All-Star lefty Justin Steele, following his major elbow surgery last year, but a flexor strain has clouded the timeline for his eventual return.

The Cubs are planning to activate Matthew Boyd during their upcoming trip, though the sharpness of their Opening Day starter is still to be determined.

After pitching for Team USA in the World Baseball Classic, Boyd spent time on the injured list to rest a strained left biceps and then recover from knee surgery, a combination of issues that has left him with a 6.00 ERA.

Edward Cabrera didn’t immediately elevate the team when he came off the injured list, giving up eight runs and failing to finish the fourth inning during Friday’s unsightly 18-3 loss to the Giants.

Besides dealing with the blister on his right middle finger, the time off was supposed to help the Cubs reset Cabrera (4.99 ERA, -0.8 WAR, per Baseball Reference) and draw out the stuff they saw when they acquired him in a big offseason trade with the Miami Marlins. Clearly, that is still a work in progress.

A functional offense would also take some pressure off Chicago’s pitching staff. Its top starter at this moment, Ben Brown, began this season in the bullpen, and he hasn’t yet completed a full year in the majors, forcing the club to proceed with even more caution.

“Unfortunately, it’s just part of it,” Taillon said. “You can do everything in your power to monitor your workload, and track everything you’re putting in your body and doing in the weight room and those types of things. Sometimes, you just land a little differently and that’s all it takes.”
